title: Elusive and real
hook: the Tao is shadowy and elusive, yet within it is something real (Tao Te Ching 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty, and your line was drifting. Did you catch yourself performing, and let your face rest? What was it like to stop keeping up? Day one thousand eighty-three.

The wind can't be held in a hand. What you get is the evidence: a flag snapping on a pole, a field of grass bending all one way, a door that slams on its own. You can't point at the thing itself, and yet nobody standing in a gale thinks it's imaginary. Some solid things in a life work like that. Trust between two old friends. The pull of a place you grew up. Hard to pin down, and hard to doubt. Chapter twenty-one of the Tao Te Ching tries to describe the Way in exactly that double sense.
screen: `NOBODY HOLDS THE WIND.` → `ONLY THE EVIDENCE.` → `HARD TO PIN, HARD TO DOUBT.`

segments.voice: First, virtue follows the Way. The chapter opens by saying that the shape of great virtue comes from following the Tao, and the Tao alone. So whatever goodness looks like, its source is this thing the chapter is about to describe. Second, shadowy and elusive. And the description is slippery on purpose. The Chinese uses a pair of words, huang and hu, that suggest something dim, flickering, glimpsed out of the corner of an eye. You look, and it slips out of sight. You reach, and it isn't where your hand lands. Third, something real inside. Then the turn. Within that dimness, the chapter says, there are forms. Within it, there are things. Deep and dark as it is, there is an essence in it, and that essence is very real. The text even says there is something trustworthy in it, a kind of proof. Elusive is not the same as empty. Fourth, how do I know? By this. The chapter ends with the speaker asking how he knows the way all things began. His answer is two words: by this. He doesn't give an argument. He points at what's in front of him, the world as it is, as if the evidence were the flag and the grass. Some readers hear in that a quiet confidence: you can't hold the Way, but you can live in its weather.
screen: `VIRTUE FOLLOWS THE WAY.` · `SHADOWY AND ELUSIVE.` · `SOMETHING REAL INSIDE.` · `HOW DO I KNOW? BY THIS.` · then, large: `ELUSIVE, AND REAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one thing you can't prove. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing you rely on without being able to show it to anyone: that a certain person means well, that rest will help, that the morning will come. Don't defend it. Just let yourself lean on it for a minute, the way you'd lean on a wall you can't see in the dark. If you pray, this may be a place for that. If you don't, the leaning is enough. The bell holds the time.
Elusive and real. Chapter twenty-one's picture of the Way: dim and slippery to the hand, with something true and trustworthy at its center. Today's word.
Your line: something real. Once today, when you notice something you can't measure, a kindness, a calm, a hunch, name it quietly to yourself as real. Day one thousand eighty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching sit with chapter twenty-one's paradox: the Way can't be grasped or seen, yet the text insists there is something real and trustworthy within it.

myth: chapter twenty-one says the Tao is elusive, so there is nothing in it
it says the opposite: within the dimness there are forms, things, and a very real essence.
the chapter ends with a long argument proving the Tao
it ends with two words: by this. the speaker points instead of arguing.
the chapter says great virtue follows the Tao
its opening line: the shape of great virtue comes from following the Tao alone.

fork.setup: you're the speaker of chapter twenty-one. someone asks how you know the way all things began. what do you say?
options: lay out a careful proof, step by step.
admit it can't be known at all.
say "by this," and point at the world in front of you.
fork.reveal: the chapter's answer is just "by this." no proof, no shrug: the evidence is what's already here.

original.note: Chinese, huǎng hū: dim, flickering, elusive. Tao Te Ching 21 uses it for the Way.

trapdoor: what you thought: elusive and real is a contradiction.
what it means: the Way slips through sight and touch, and still has a real, trustworthy essence inside it.
what a scholar hears: huang hu, the dim and flickering, paired with jing, an essence, which the chapter calls very real, and an ending that answers only: by this.

notes: Chapter 21 is paraphrased throughout: great virtue following the Tao alone; the Tao as 恍惚 (dim, elusive); forms (象), things (物) and an essence (精) within it; the essence very real (甚真), with something trustworthy (信) in it; the closing 'how do I know... by this' (以此). Confirm.

'Legge's translation turns it into rhyme: our sight it flies, our touch as well' is given without quotation marks because the exact Legge wording was not verified. Legge's chapter 21 is in verse; if the line is confirmed as 'Our sight it flies, our touch as well', it could be quoted.
The hook's trust and home examples are general illustrations, not claims from the text.
The wind image is an illustration, not a source.
